As AI reshapes insurance sales, BCG argues that insurers should prioritize assisted distribution: using AI to strengthen human advisors now while building the data, workflows, and governance needed for more autonomous selling later.

Assisted distribution improves both advisor capacity and conversionAI can free 15%–25% of advisor time from preparation and administration, while improving lead selection, personalization, and follow-up—creating more customer conversations and making each one more productive.

The greatest gains come from redesigning the full sales journeyRather than automate isolated tasks, insurers should embed AI before, during, and after meetings. One Asian life insurer raised sales productivity 20%–30% by combining knowledge support, next-best actions, and tailored sales narratives.

Human judgment remains central even as AI assumes routine workAI should handle analysis, documents, customer signals, and routine interactions so advisors can focus on trust, suitability, and complex advice. A second insurer generated 1 million personalized advisor nudges daily, achieving a 40% click-through rate.

Scaling assisted distribution is the practical route to autonomyThe harder challenge is organizational, not technical: roughly 70% of the effort involves people and processes. Insurers must establish decision rights, exception handling, security, and responsible-AI controls before agents transact independently.

AI is pushing insurance distribution toward a new operating model, taking on meaningful parts of the advice and sales process, from identifying opportunities and preparing advisors to supporting recommendations and follow-ups. These advances are paving the way to a more autonomous model in which AI agents interact directly with customers and, eventually, other AI agents.For now, the bigger priority for insurers is assisted distribution, where AI works with human advisors, taking on more of the preparation, analysis, administration, and routine customer interactions, freeing advisors to focus on judgment, advice, and high-value conversations. This middle phase of a three-part evolution stands between today’s augmented distribution, where AI operates in the background, and an autonomous future. (See Exhibit 1.) In the near term, assisted distribution can increase both the number and effectiveness of customer interactions, with BCG project experience indicating that distribution productivity could increase by 30% to 50%. Over time, it will help insurers build the capabilities required for autonomous distribution.

The Economics of Assisted Distribution
The productivity potential comes from two mutually reinforcing levers: creating more opportunities for advisors to engage customers and increasing the value of each interaction. (See Exhibit 2.) The first effect is more “times at bat.” By taking on the administrative and preparatory work surrounding the sales process, AI can free up advisor capacity for customer-facing activity. BCG project experience suggests that assisted distribution can release 15% to 25% of advisor time, creating room for more client meetings and more selling opportunities.

The second effect is a higher “batting average.” AI can improve how advisors use customer-facing time by helping them focus on higher-intent leads, enter meetings better prepared, tailor recommendations more effectively, and follow up more consistently. The potential improvement in the effectiveness of advisor time is 15% to 20%.Together, these benefits can lift overall productivity by 30% to 50%, based on BCG experience. The value is not simply lower operating cost. It is a better economic model for advice: more customer-facing capacity, combined with greater effectiveness in each interaction.

Reimagining the Sales Journey End to End
Capturing the full value of assisted distribution requires redesigning the sales journey, not merely automating isolated tasks. AI can support the advisor at each stage—before, during, and after the customer interaction. (See Exhibit 3.) In lead generation, it can help focus advisors on the highest-intent prospects. In meeting preparation, it can assemble client briefs, prepopulate documents, and provide coaching. During the meeting, recommendations can adapt in real time as underwriting pre-checks run in the background.

The same principle extends beyond the meeting itself. AI can automatically capture CRM updates, action items, and issuance communications, reducing the administrative burden that typically follows a customer interaction. It can also make engagement more timely by using life-event and lapse signals to trigger personalized outreach—an approach that can support always-on retention and customer engagement rather than relying primarily on scheduled or reactive contact.What matters is the cumulative effect across the customer journey. As AI takes on more of the preparation, analysis, and routine execution, advisors can concentrate on the work where human judgment, trust, and advice matter most. The result is not simply a faster version of the existing process but a different division of labor between people and AI, designed around higher-value customer interaction.An Asian life insurer illustrates what an end-to-end approach can look like in practice. Seeking to generate further growth in its existing market, the insurer introduced an AI-assisted solution that boosted advisors’ capacity and effectiveness. To enable more “times at bat,” a knowledge assistant helped advisors find answers to complex policy questions faster, while automation reduced routine work such as preparing meeting summaries. To raise advisors’ “batting average,” a next-best-action engine identified products with the highest purchase propensity, while customer-specific sales narratives helped make client conversations more relevant.These capabilities were embedded in advisors’ day-to-day work and supported by a feedback loop in which data gathered from customers and advisors improved subsequent recommendations and actions. The impact included 20% to 30% improvements in sales productivity and a meaningful increase in first- and second-year customer retention.Another Asian life insurer developed solutions to relay personalized nudges aimed at developing advisors and strengthening behaviors that lead to better sales outcomes. The system generated 1 million unique nudges a day, with the advisors’ click-through rate reaching 40%.AI-Assisted Distribution Builds the Foundation for Autonomy
The case for assisted distribution extends beyond near-term productivity. To make human-AI collaboration work at scale, insurers must build capabilities that will also underpin autonomous distribution: connected data and systems, redesigned workflows, clear decision rights, stronger governance, and frontline adoption.The challenge is not primarily technological. In BCG’s experience, approximately 70% of a company’s effort should be focused on people and processes. Insurers need to determine where AI acts, where people intervene, how exceptions are handled, and how frontline teams will work differently. They also need to build monitoring and security to make those new workflows dependable at scale. Making these changes part of the journey from pilot to scale—rather than treating them as downstream implementation issues—is essential to realizing the value of assisted distribution.That is what makes assisted distribution a no-regret move. The pace of autonomy will vary by market, product, and distribution model, and many advice-intensive businesses are likely to retain a substantial human role for some time. But insurers do not need certainty about the eventual end state before acting. By building the capabilities required for assisted distribution now, they can capture material value in the near term while putting themselves in a stronger position to move toward greater autonomy as technology, regulation, and customer behavior evolve.The practical agenda is two-track: scale assisted distribution now to capture near-term value, while beginning low-regret preparations for greater autonomy. (See “Preparing for Autonomous Distribution.”)

Preparing for Autonomous Distribution

Assisted distribution should be the near-term priority, but insurers also need to prepare for a future in which AI agents play a more direct role in how customers discover, evaluate, and purchase insurance. That preparation has three dimensions: ensuring that insurers are discoverable, can engage customers conversationally, and can ultimately support transactional interactions.Be discoverable. Insurers need to make sure their products, propositions, and information are visible to the AI assistants customers increasingly use to search and compare options. In an AI-mediated market, discoverability becomes a distribution capability in its own right.Be conversational. Insurers will also need customer-facing AI capabilities that can answer questions, explain products, gather information, and guide customers through their own channels.Be transactional. Over time, the interaction may move beyond discovery and conversation toward execution, with external AI agents able to obtain quotes and complete transactions with an insurer’s AI agents.As autonomy increases, so does the importance of responsible AI. Insurers need to embed explainability, suitability, privacy, auditability, security, and clear accountability for AI-driven decisions into the operating model and technology architecture from the outset.

The path to autonomous distribution will not be a single leap. Insurers that make assisted distribution work now can improve the economics of human advice while building the data, technology, operating-model, and governance capabilities that an autonomous model will require. That gives assisted distribution strategic value beyond near-term productivity gains: it allows insurers to learn where AI can take on more responsibility, where human judgment remains essential, and how the two should work together at scale. Insurers that move deliberately through this phase will be better positioned to capture value today and adapt as distribution becomes increasingly AI-mediated.
